fig1_flow_energy_terms.svg: The flow energy carried across a control surface is $\psi=h+V^2/2+gz$ (flow_energy), but the last two terms are almost always negligible. Measured against superheated steam at 60 bar, 400 $^\circ$C ($h=3177$ kJ/kg from steam table A-4), the velocity must exceed $\sim$250 m/s before kinetic energy reaches 1% of $h$, and a 300 m elevation change contributes only 0.09%. This is the arithmetic behind the standard phrase 'kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible' — and the warning that in a nozzle, where $V$ is the whole point, it is not.
fig2_nozzle_exit_velocity.svg: A nozzle is the control volume where the kinetic term is the point. With no shaft work and no heat transfer the steady-flow energy balance gives $V_{out}=\sqrt{V_{in}^2+2\,\Delta h}$ (nozzle_exit_velocity, the factor $10^3$ converting kJ/kg to J/kg). Because the dependence is a square root, the three inlet velocities converge: by a 200 kJ/kg drop an inlet at 100 m/s exits only 1.2% faster than one starting from rest. A modest enthalpy drop buys a very large velocity — 632 m/s from 200 kJ/kg.
